name: Umbra Collective Sensor-Blind Cap
description:
A baseball-style cap with an IR LED array embedded in the brim that floods facial-recognition cameras with invisible light, rendering the wearer's face unreadable to automated systems. To human eyes, the cap looks completely normal. To cameras, the wearer's face is a white-out blur.

Sold openly in Shelf markets as a 'privacy accessory' and quietly tolerated by most security forces who consider it a nuisance rather than a threat. Higher-tier zones with military-grade surveillance systems can compensate for the IR flooding, limiting the cap's effectiveness to mid- and lower-tier districts.
functionality: IR camera blinding, facial recognition defeat (effective against civilian-grade systems)
what_it_says: You paid Φ90 to become invisible to every cheap camera on the street. Best investment you ever made.
story_hooks: A politician is photographed buying Sensor-Blind Caps in bulk — raising questions about who they're distributing them to and why they want those people invisible.

physical_description.visual_profile: A deceptively mundane baseball cap with a slightly thicker, subtly reinforced brim. The crown sits comfortably rounded, the bill projects at a standard angle. To naked eyes, it reads as ordinary streetwear—nothing that triggers a second glance. The real technology is invisible: an embedded IR LED array hidden within the brim's structure that only cameras can detect.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed, adjustable. Six-panel crown with a structured but not aggressive bill. Sits naturally on the head without drawing attention. Back closure is a friction-fit fabric strap with discrete micro-adjustment, designed to feel like standard cap hardware.
physical_description.primary_material: Ballistic-grade synthetic weave base (IR-transparent polymer composite) with embedded nano-LED circuitry in the brim. The outer facing is brushed cotton-poly blend to maintain authentic appearance. Inner band is moisture-wicking tech-fabric.
physical_description.texture: Smooth, well-worn aesthetic on the exterior—no visible seams or technological hints. The brim has subtle quilting to conceal the LED array channels. Feels like quality streetwear: soft, broken-in, unremarkable.
physical_description.color_scheme: Neutral palette—charcoal grey, black, or faded indigo as primary colors. Minimal branding: a small embroidered Φ symbol on the side or a woven Umbra Collective tag on the back that looks like any other cap maker's mark. The embedded tech is infrared-spectrum only; completely invisible to human color perception.
physical_description.closures: Friction-fit back strap with micro-adjustment, mimics standard baseball cap hardware. No visible zippers or tech ports. The power cell (microbattery) is sealed within the brim structure; designed for 72-hour continuous operation between charges.
distinctive_features: IR LED array embedded in brim—floods facial-recognition systems with invisible light, rendering face unreadable to automated cameras
Completely invisible to human eyes when powered; cap appears entirely normal
Micro-battery power cell sealed in brim structure
Discrete Umbra Collective branding—subtle enough to avoid drawing corpo security attention
Friction-fit adjustment—no exposed tech ports or charging contacts
Brushed finish exterior eliminates glint or reflection that might hint at embedded systems
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3-4 accessible privacy tech. Openly sold in Shelf markets at Φ180–250 range. Working-class price point, but signals privacy-conscious behavior. Tier 2 zones tolerate it grudgingly; Tier 1 corporate zones have countermeasures.
physical_description.cultural_context: Signals someone who values anonymity in public spaces—street-oriented, privacy-conscious, possibly involved in informal economy or just paranoid about corpo surveillance. Common among couriers, freelance netrunners, activists, and general privacy advocates. Not inherently illegal, but wearing it marks you as someone who thinks about being watched.
physical_description.condition_typical: Broken-in and unremarkable. A well-worn cap shows creasing in the crown, slight fading on the bill, possibly some dust or scuff marks. This anonymity is the point—a pristine new cap would paradoxically draw attention. Most owners prefer the cap to look like it's been in rotation for months.
